trial_name: GASTROSAM — Intravenous Rehydration for Severe Acute Malnutrition with Gastroenteritis (2025)
citation: Maitland K, Ouattara SM, Sainna H, et al. Intravenous Rehydration for Severe Acute Malnutrition with Gastroenteritis. N Engl J Med. 2025;393(13):1257-1268
trial_type: Multicentre, open-label, randomised, factorial, superiority trial
one_liner: In children with severe acute malnutrition and severe dehydration, IV rehydration with Ringer's lactate did not reduce mortality compared to cautious oral/nasogastric strategy, did not cause fluid overload, but increased hypokalaemia, requiring careful monitoring.

pico.population: Children aged 6 months to 12 years with severe acute malnutrition, acute gastroenteritis, and WHO-defined severe dehydration in sub-Saharan African hospitals.
pico.intervention: Intravenous rehydration with Ringer's lactate 100 ml/kg (rapid or slow); factorial assignment to ReSoMal vs standard WHO ORS.
pico.comparison: Cautious oral/nasogastric rehydration strategy (5 ml/kg every 30 min for 2h, then 5-10 ml/kg hourly alternating with F-75).
pico.outcome: Death by 96 hours (primary); secondary included 28-day mortality, fluid overload events, and electrolyte abnormalities.

background.existing_knowledge: Children with SAM and acute gastroenteritis often have severe dehydration and electrolyte derangements; international guidance favoured cautious oral/nasogastric strategies due to fear of fluid overload.
background.knowledge_gap: No RCT had directly compared standard-volume IV rehydration to cautious oral/nasogastric strategy for severe dehydration in SAM; undertreatment of hypovolaemia might contribute to high mortality.
background.hypothesis: IV rehydration with Ringer's lactate 100 ml/kg would reduce 96-hour mortality without increasing fluid overload.

methods.design: Multicentre, open-label, randomised, factorial, superiority trial (2:1:1 allocation: oral strategy vs rapid IV vs slow IV).
methods.setting: 6 hospitals in Kenya, Uganda, Niger, Nigeria.

inclusion: Severe acute malnutrition (weight-for-height z-score < -3, MUAC < 11.5 cm, and/or bilateral pedal oedema)
Acute gastroenteritis (≥3 loose stools per day)
Severe dehydration per WHO criteria (≥2 signs: lethargy/unconsciousness, sunken eyes, inability to drink/drinking poorly, skin pinch returning very slowly)
exclusion: Known congenital or rheumatic heart disease

methods.intervention: IV rehydration with Ringer's lactate 100 ml/kg, either rapid (over 3h if <12 months, 6h if ≥12 months) or slow (over 8h); factorial assignment to ReSoMal vs standard WHO ORS. Shock management: rapid arm permitted bolus 20 ml/kg; slow arm no bolus.
methods.comparison: Cautious oral/nasogastric rehydration: ORS 5 ml/kg every 30 min for 2h, then 5-10 ml/kg hourly for 4-10h, alternating with F-75; shock allowed bolus 15 ml/kg; factorial to ReSoMal vs standard ORS.
methods.blinding: Open-label for clinicians; laboratory analyses performed with blinding to treatment assignment.
methods.sample_size_power: 272 children required to detect 30% relative reduction in 96-hour mortality (assumed 58% vs 41%) with 80% power at 5% significance.
secondary_outcomes: Deterioration in level of consciousness or seizures (suspected cerebral oedema)
Change in serum sodium and potassium from baseline
methods.follow_up: Intensive clinical monitoring for first 8 hours; biochemical sampling at randomisation, 8 hours, and 24 hours; mortality assessed at 96 hours and 28 days, plus day-7 follow-up.

headline_bullets: 96-hour mortality was similar between IV 7% and oral 8% (RR 1.02; 95% CI 0.41-2.52; P=0.69).
No cases of pulmonary oedema or heart failure occurred in any group (0/272), challenging the main safety concern.
IV rehydration corrected hyponatraemia faster but increased early severe hypokalaemia (45% vs 31% at 8h), demanding potassium management.

outcomes_table.outcome: Deterioration in consciousness or seizures (suspected cerebral oedema)

outcomes_table.note: Sodium correction faster in IV arms.
Persistent potassium vulnerability in IV arms.

outcomes_table.outcome: Change in serum sodium from baseline to 8 hours (mmol/L)
Change in serum potassium from baseline to 8 hours (mmol/L)

safety: No pulmonary oedema or heart failure reported in any of the 272 participants.
Serious adverse events numerically lower in IV arms (18% vs 23%; OR 0.73, 95% CI 0.40-1.32).
Suspected cerebral oedema or seizures: 4% IV vs 7% oral (OR 0.54, 95% CI 0.24-1.23).
Severe hyponatraemia at 8h reduced with IV (16% vs 45%; OR 0.23, 95% CI 0.13-0.41).
Severe hypokalaemia at 8h increased with IV (45% vs 31%; OR 1.79, 95% CI 1.07-3.01).
At 24h, severe hyponatraemia remained lower with IV (17% vs 27%; OR 0.53, 95% CI 0.29-0.98); severe hypokalaemia remained higher (29% vs 20%; OR 1.59, 95% CI 0.89-2.83).

domains.notes: Sealed opaque envelopes with block sequences and site stratification (2:1:1); good allocation concealment.
Open-label for clinicians; primary outcome (mortality) is objective; lab analyses were blinded, reducing detection bias for biochemical endpoints.
Minimal loss to follow-up: 271/272 at 96h, 270/272 at 28 days; intention-to-treat analysis performed.
IV fluid receipt within 24h: oral arm 22% vs IV arms 99%; this rescue IV use likely attenuates between-group contrast for efficacy.
Groups comparable (median age ~13-14 mo, weight ~6.0 kg, kwashiorkor ~48-51%). High prevalence of baseline severe hyponatraemia (45-53%) and hypokalaemia (40-49%).
Multicentre (4 countries, 6 sites); analyses adjusted for site, but site-level variation in care may still exist.
IV dosing prespecified at 100 ml/kg; bolus policies differed by arm (oral 15 ml/kg for shock, rapid IV 20 ml/kg, slow IV no bolus), potentially affecting early rescue in the sickest.
Mortality is objective; adverse events relied on clinical judgement without routine imaging, susceptible to ascertainment bias.
ITT with site-adjusted models; wide confidence intervals for mortality reflect limited precision.

internal_validity.verdict: Moderate: strong randomisation, minimal attrition, and objective primary outcome, but open-label and rescue IV use dilute efficacy contrasts.

domains.notes: Typical of complicated SAM admissions in sub-Saharan Africa; excluded congenital heart disease and diarrhoea >14 days, limiting generalisability to those subgroups.
Trial conducted in research-capable hospitals with close monitoring and biochemistry; generalisability to facilities without reliable lab monitoring and potassium supplementation may be limited.

external_validity.verdict: Findings likely applicable to similar low-resource inpatient settings with capacity for electrolyte monitoring and management; implementation in less-equipped settings requires explicit potassium protocols.

strengths: Directly addresses a long-standing, practice-defining safety concern with a pragmatic RCT in high-burden settings.
Clinically meaningful primary endpoint (96-hour mortality) with very low loss to follow-up.
Frequent monitoring and blinded lab endpoints enabled detailed safety phenotyping (fluid overload and electrolyte trajectories).
Included two IV delivery rates (rapid vs slow) supporting internal comparison of infusion speed.
limitations: Open-label design and protocol-driven rescue IV use in the oral arm reduce treatment separation and may dilute between-group efficacy differences.
Safety outcomes relied on clinical recognition; subtle pulmonary or cardiac overload could be under-recognised.
Reliance on laboratory monitoring and potassium supplementation infrastructure that is not universally available in all low-resource settings.
Multicentre variation in supportive care may influence outcomes.

critical_appraisal.summary: GASTROSAM provides moderate-quality evidence that IV rehydration with Ringer's lactate does not reduce short-term mortality in SAM with severe dehydration but is safe with respect to fluid overload; the trade-off is a higher risk of hypokalaemia, highlighting the need for bundled electrolyte monitoring and supplementation.
strengths: Well-designed multicentre RCT with strong randomisation and minimal attrition.
Pragmatic inclusion of two IV rates within the intervention arm.
weaknesses: Open-label nature increases risk of co-intervention and ascertainment bias for subjective safety endpoints.
Substantial crossover (22%) to IV in the oral arm attenuates the efficacy contrast.
Adverse events diagnosed clinically without imaging.
Wide confidence intervals limit precision for mortality differences.

sections.authors_conclusion: In children with SAM and WHO-defined severe dehydration, IV rehydration with Ringer's lactate did not reduce mortality, was not associated with fluid overload, but increased early severe hypokalaemia; therefore, careful potassium management is essential.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: IV rehydration can be considered as an option in SAM with severe dehydration when oral/nasogastric strategy is not feasible or insufficient, provided electrolyte monitoring and supplementation are in place.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: Hospitalized children aged 6 months to 12 years with SAM, acute gastroenteritis, and WHO severe dehydration, in settings with capacity for laboratory monitoring and potassium replacement.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: That IV rehydration is superior or mandatory; oral/nasogastric rehydration remains a safe and effective strategy, and the choice depends on local context and resources.
implementation_caveats: Close monitoring of potassium is essential; routine potassium supplementation should be considered when using Ringer's lactate.
Protocols for electrolyte monitoring and correction must be in place before adopting routine IV rehydration in this population.
Cautious oral/nasogastric rehydration remains appropriate where monitoring is limited.

controversies.notes: Editorial highlighted that GASTROSAM provides direct evidence against the assumption that IV rehydration inevitably precipitates fluid overload, while emphasising the need for system readiness (monitoring and electrolyte management).

controversies.topic: Electrolyte safety debate (potassium risk with balanced crystalloids)
controversies.notes: Correspondence raised concern that potassium-free balanced solutions (Ringer's lactate) may worsen hypokalaemia in a population with profound baseline deficits, arguing that fluid selection and/or potassium supplementation strategy should be explicit.

controversies.topic: Generalisability and 'trial care' versus routine ward care
controversies.notes: Correspondence emphasised that improved outcomes and safety may depend on broader care-system strengthening (staffing, monitoring, access to electrolytes) and queried whether results can be replicated where these elements are inconsistent.
Pre-trial systematic review evidence was limited, creating uncertainty about efficacy and safety, which justified randomisation.

controversies.topic: Positioning relative to earlier African paediatric fluid trials
controversies.notes: FEAST and earlier phase II rehydration trials informed safety monitoring but did not address SAM-specific safety concerns; GASTROSAM provides SAM-specific data.
The primary report described factorial assignment to ReSoMal vs standard WHO ORS, but comparative outcomes for this component were not reported.

context_related_trials.relation: A landmark African paediatric fluid trial that showed harm from fluid boluses in children with shock without severe malnutrition; relevant mechanistically but differs in population (no SAM) and intervention (bolus vs rehydration).
Informed feasibility and safety monitoring frameworks for fluid delivery rate and physiologic response, but did not resolve SAM-specific safety concerns.

unresolved_questions: Optimal fluid type and potassium supplementation strategy for IV rehydration in SAM.
Effectiveness and safety of IV rehydration in settings without laboratory monitoring.
Results of the ReSoMal vs standard ORS factorial component (not yet reported).
Impact of IV rehydration speed (rapid vs slow) on clinical outcomes beyond electrolyte effects.

numbers_to_remember: Severe hypokalaemia at 8h: 45% IV vs 31% oral
No pulmonary oedema or heart failure in any arm (0/272)
quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: In SAM with severe dehydration, IV rehydration didn't reduce mortality but appears safe regarding fluid overload; however, it increases hypokalaemia, making potassium monitoring and supplementation mandatory.
